the_asymmetry_being_closed.core_side_detail: core/__init__.py is docstring-only and contains no import statement of any kind. If a future change added an eager import of an L3 module to it, the static detector would see that import and report it as a fresh L1 -> L3 forbidden edge, because the file would then be classified L1. The reclassification makes the core side MORE sensitive to regression, not less: the very act that would invalidate the reclassification is the act the existing gate already catches. No new test is needed to hold this invariant.
the_asymmetry_being_closed.data_layer_side_detail: data_layer/__init__.py holds its L1-ness by a PEP 562 module-level __getattr__ that resolves 'data_layer.config', 'data_layer.models' and 'data_layer.sqlite' through importlib.import_module on STRING module names. tools.build_architecture_inventory._resolve_imports walks the AST for ast.Import and ast.ImportFrom nodes; an importlib.import_module call with a string argument is neither, so the detector is structurally blind to it. A future regression that added another importlib-string L2 target at import time could therefore leave the gate reporting green while data_layer/__init__.py, now labelled L1, actually loads L2 infrastructure. That is precisely the failure mode the ARCH-EDGE-001 artifact recorded as its contingency caveat, and precisely what this condition exists to prevent.

what_closed_means.must_be_a_runtime_behavioural_check_note: A test that greps data_layer/__init__.py for the substring 'import', that asserts the file is under N lines, that asserts _LAZY_ATTRIBUTES has a particular literal content, or that merely re-runs find_forbidden_edges, does NOT satisfy this condition. Every one of those is another static check and every one of them is blind to exactly the regression class this condition targets. The check must observe what the interpreter actually loads.
what_closed_means.required_observable: Importing data_layer - and importing an L1 submodule of it, which necessarily executes data_layer/__init__.py first - must be shown NOT to have loaded any data_layer module that the architecture map classifies L2, measured against real interpreter state. The measurement must be taken in a CLEAN subprocess interpreter and compared against that subprocess's own baseline sys.modules, so that modules already imported by the pytest process cannot mask, pre-satisfy, or fake the result.
what_closed_means.must_derive_the_forbidden_set_note: The set of L2 data_layer modules must be read from packaging/atlas_architecture_map.json at test time. A hardcoded list of today's L2 submodules would silently fail to cover one added later, which is the same contingency the test exists to remove.
what_closed_means.must_be_proven_to_discriminate_note: A test that passes is not evidence until it has been shown to FAIL against the behaviour it claims to forbid. The implementer must construct the regressed behaviour under controlled conditions - a fixture, a synthetic package, or a temporary copy - and demonstrate the check failing against it, then demonstrate it passing against the real current implementation. Editing the real data_layer/__init__.py to produce the failure is NOT authorized: source is read-only under this grant, and a discrimination proof that mutates production source is a worse instrument than the gap it is closing.

the_distinction.permitted_exception: An entry in permitted_exceptions names a specific importer/imported PAIR and tells the detector to stop reporting it. The layer labels stay as they are, the edge is conceded to be a real cross-layer dependency, and the gate is told to tolerate it. It changes the GATE.
the_distinction.weakening_a_forbidden_edge_rule: Deleting or narrowing an entry in forbidden_edges - for example removing L4 -> L2 - would stop the detector reporting an entire CLASS of edge. It changes the RULE.
the_distinction.reclassification: Correcting a module's layer label changes neither the gate nor the rule. Every forbidden_edges entry remains exactly as written and keeps its full force; permitted_exceptions gains nothing. What changes is one input fact: which layer a given file belongs to. It changes the LABEL.

why_the_label_was_wrong.core_init: core/__init__.py was never classified L3 by a judgement about core/__init__.py. It fell through to the generic 'core/*' -> L3 default, whose own recorded reason is 'application-layer orchestration, per the composition-root diagram in core/application.py's own docstring'. That reason is true of core/application.py, core/market_loop.py and core/brain.py. It is not true of a six-line file containing a docstring and nothing else. A file that orchestrates nothing, imports nothing and executes nothing is not application orchestration. L1 - domain vocabulary, no I/O - is the accurate label, and the map already carries roughly thirty per-file L1 exceptions to this same generic core/* default (core/decision.py, core/risk_engine.py, core/position_sizing.py, core/fee_accounting.py and others), each recorded for the same reason: the generic default did not describe the file.
why_the_label_was_wrong.data_layer_init: data_layer/__init__.py's L2 classification has an explicit recorded reason inside the generic 'data_layer/*' rule: 'data_layer/__init__.py itself re-exports both L1 (models) and L2 (config, sqlite) symbols so is classified at the lower-common-denominator L2'. That reasoning was correct when written, for an __init__ that eagerly re-exported. It is no longer descriptive of the file: the re-exports are lazy, resolved per attribute on first access, and the file's own docstring states this was deliberate precisely so that importing any data_layer submodule does not drag in the L2 SQLite backend. Measured behaviour confirms it - importing data_layer.contracts loads data_layer and data_layer.contracts and nothing else. Lower-common-denominator is the right rule for a file that actually loads both; it is the wrong rule for a file that loads neither until asked. The label is stale relative to the code, and correcting a stale label is the ordinary maintenance of a classification artifact, not an erosion of the rules that read it.

forbidden_edges_l4_to_l2_and_l4_to_l3_no.what_actually_happens_to_group_c: The three Group C edges do not become tolerated L4 -> L3 / L4 -> L2 edges. The reported violation was entirely against the PARENT packages Python executes on the way, and once those parents carry their accurate L1 labels the traversal is L4 -> L1 at every step: a permitted dependency, not a tolerated forbidden one.
forbidden_edges_l4_to_l2_and_l4_to_l3_no.the_test_that_this_reasoning_must_surviv: If a future change made either __init__ genuinely reach L2 or L3 - eagerly on the core side, eagerly or by importlib string on the data_layer side - the research-cannot-trade edge would be real again, and something must catch it. On the data_layer side the detector cannot, which is exactly why condition 2 makes the compensating test binding rather than advisory. The claim that this grant does not weaken the research-cannot-trade boundary is only honest BECAUSE that test is a condition of the grant; without it the claim would be false and the grant should not be given.
